items.prompt: A function performs one full scan of n elements followed by another full scan of n elements. What is the tight asymptotic time?

options.text: O(n).
O(n²).
O(log n).

feedback.reason: The two scans run one after the other, so their work adds to n + n = 2n rather than multiplying.
feedback.details: Count executions of the scan body. The first pass visits n elements and the second pass visits another n, for 2n visits. Big-O describes how that count grows as n grows: multiplying n by the constant 2 does not change the growth class, so the tight asymptotic bound is Θ(n), commonly written O(n). Multiplication would be justified only if one full scan happened inside every iteration of the other.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.quadratic: Sequential phases add rather than multiply.

items.prompt: An outer loop runs n times and an inner loop runs n times for every outer iteration. What structure determines the time bound?

options.text: The iteration counts multiply, yielding n·n operations.
The counts add because the loops are written on separate lines.
The variable names determine the bound.
The inner loop is constant because its body is small.

feedback.reason: Every one of the n outer iterations triggers a fresh inner loop of n iterations, so the body runs n × n times.
feedback.details: Start with one outer iteration: it performs n inner-body executions. The same n executions occur for each of the n outer iterations, giving n·n = n² executions in total. The body being short affects only a constant factor; it does not remove repetitions. By contrast, two loops that run consecutively would add their costs instead of multiplying them.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum: The inner loop executes inside every outer iteration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Names have no effect on execution count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: A small body still repeats n² times.

items.prompt: A nested loop has inner index j start at i and run to n - 1. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The total iterations form a triangular sum and are O(n²).
The total is O(n) because j never restarts at zero.
Any nested loop with changing bounds is O(n³).
The shrinking inner loop makes total work constant.

feedback.reason: As i increases, the inner loop gets shorter, but its total work is still the triangular sum n + (n − 1) + … + 1.
feedback.details: For i = 0, the inner loop has n iterations; for i = 1, it has n − 1; eventually it has one. Adding those counts gives n(n + 1)/2. Dividing by 2 changes only a constant factor, while the n² term remains, so the running time is Θ(n²). A shrinking inner loop is not automatically linear; you must add all of its lengths.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_cubic: There are only two loop dimensions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: The total still grows with n.

items.prompt: A loop repeatedly divides a positive integer n by 2 until it reaches zero. What drives the iteration count?

options.text: The number of times n can be halved, which is O(log n).
Exactly n iterations.
Exactly one iteration.
The division operator makes the loop O(n²).

feedback.reason: Each iteration halves the remaining value, so after k iterations it is n / 2^k; reaching 1 therefore needs only logarithmically many halvings.
feedback.details: Write out the sequence: n, n/2, n/4, n/8, and so on. After k halvings the value is n/2^k. The loop ends once that value is below 1, which is equivalent to 2^k being at least n. Solving for k gives log₂ n. The important signal is multiplicative shrinkage: subtracting one would take linear time, but repeatedly dividing by a fixed factor takes logarithmic time.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.numeric_n: The value shrinks multiplicatively, not by one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: Inputs larger than one require multiple halvings.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.quadratic: Operator choice does not determine the number of iterations.

items.prompt: Two pointers each move only forward through an array, and neither pointer moves backward. Why can a nested while loop still be O(n)?

options.text: Across the whole run, each pointer advances at most n times.
Nested loops are always linear.
Variables named left and right imply O(n).
The loop body is constant-time, so total time is constant.

feedback.reason: The nested shape is misleading here: each pointer only moves forward and can advance at most n times during the entire run.
feedback.details: Do not count the inner loop as n for every outer iteration unless it restarts. Instead, charge each iteration to a pointer advance. A left pointer can advance at most n positions and a right-moving pointer can also advance at most n positions, so there are at most 2n advances. If every loop iteration makes at least one such advance, there can be only O(n) iterations overall. This aggregate argument fails if an inner pointer resets and revisits the same elements for every outer iteration.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nested_never_matters: Nested loops can be quadratic when inner work resets.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant_body: The body still executes multiple times.

items.prompt: A loop may break on the first element, but in the worst case it scans all n elements. What is the worst-case time?

options.text: O(n).
O(1) because an early break exists.
O(log n) because the loop can stop early.
O(n²) because there are two outcomes.

feedback.reason: Worst-case analysis asks for the valid input of size n that makes the algorithm do the most work, and that input can delay the break until the final element.
feedback.details: An early break proves that some inputs finish quickly; it does not bound every input. For a worst-case example, choose an array where the sought value is absent or appears last. The loop then executes its body n times, so the worst-case bound is Θ(n). That first-element break belongs to the best-case discussion, not to a claim that the algorithm is constant time.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: Worst-case analysis uses an input that delays the break.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.logarithmic: Early termination alone does not imply halving.

items.prompt: A function sorts n values and then scans them once. Which term dominates the total time under comparison sorting?

options.text: O(n log n).
O(n) because the final scan is visible in the return path.
O(n² log n) because phases multiply.
O(1) because sorting is a library call.

feedback.reason: Sorting costs O(n log n) and the later scan costs O(n), so sequential composition gives O(n log n + n).
feedback.details: Both phases execute, so add their costs first. For large n, n log n grows faster than n because log n eventually exceeds every fixed constant. Therefore the sort dominates the scan and the total is Θ(n log n). A library call is not free: its complexity must be included unless the problem explicitly treats it as a constant-time primitive.

items.prompt: Why is the statement "the loop variable is named i, so the loop is O(n)" invalid?

options.text: Complexity follows the loop's update rule, bounds, and work, not the variable name.
The name i is reserved for logarithmic loops.
Every loop is O(n) regardless of its header.
Longer variable names increase the iteration count.

feedback.reason: The name i carries no execution information: it could increase by one, double each time, reset inside another loop, or follow another variable.
feedback.details: Complexity comes from a count, not from a naming convention. Inspect the initial value, update rule, stopping condition, and work per iteration. For example, `i += 1` from 0 to n performs about n iterations, while `i *= 2` from 1 to n performs about log n; both variables may be named i. A nested loop can also reset i and make the total quadratic. Derive the bound from behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.all_loops_linear: Loops can be constant, logarithmic, quadratic, or other.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names_affect_cpu: Names do not alter the algorithm's execution model.

items.prompt: Which rules are valid when combining time costs? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sequential phases add their costs.
Independent nested iteration counts multiply.
Lower-order terms and constant factors can be dropped for asymptotic classification.
Variable names determine which term dominates.

feedback.reason: The valid rules describe how real executions compose: consecutive phases add, repeated inner work multiplies when it is independent, and asymptotic notation keeps the dominant growth term.
feedback.details: Use the rules in order. Count each phase, add phases that run one after another, and multiply only when one count repeats fully for every execution of another. Once you have an expression such as 3n² + 5n, constants and lower-order terms can be removed for the asymptotic class, yielding Θ(n²). Variable names are never an input to this calculation; they do not change how often the program runs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_names: Names do not encode operation counts.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sequential_add: All phases execute one after another.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.nested_multiply: The inner work repeats for each outer iteration.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.dominant_term: They do not change growth class.

items.prompt: Which loop patterns can be O(n) despite containing nested syntax? Select all that apply.

options.text: An inner pointer advances monotonically and never resets across outer iterations.
Each input element is processed by the inner body at most a constant number of times overall.
The inner loop scans all n elements from the beginning for every outer iteration.
Each item is pushed once and popped once across all iterations.

feedback.reason: Nested syntax is linear when the inner work is shared across the whole run rather than restarted for every outer iteration.
feedback.details: Ask whether an element can be charged only a constant number of times. A monotonic inner pointer never returns to an earlier element, so all of its advances together are bounded by n. Likewise, an item pushed once and popped once contributes at most two stack operations. A full inner scan that resets to the beginning for every outer iteration has no such shared bound: it performs n work n times, or Θ(n²).

items.prompt: Which facts are needed to derive a recursive time bound? Select all that apply.

options.text: How many recursive subproblems each call creates.
How the input size changes in each child.
How much nonrecursive work one call performs.
Whether the function is named solve or dfs.

feedback.reason: A recursive time bound needs the number of child calls, their input sizes, and the nonrecursive work done by the current call.
feedback.details: These facts form a recurrence such as T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n. The number of children controls branching, child size controls recursion depth, and local work must be paid at every node in the recursion tree. Knowing only that a function calls itself is insufficient: one child of size n−1 behaves very differently from two children of size n/2, even if both functions are named `dfs` or `solve`.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.subproblem_size: Depth and total nodes depend on shrinkage.

items.prompt: Which analyses correctly distinguish best, average, amortized, and worst case? Select all that apply.

options.text: Worst case considers the maximum work over inputs of a given size.
Best case considers the minimum work over inputs of a given size.
Average case requires an input distribution or probability model.
Amortized analysis is the same as expected time under random inputs.

feedback.reason: Best, worst, average, and amortized case use different quantifiers, so evidence for one is not automatically evidence for another.
feedback.details: Worst case is the maximum work over valid inputs of a fixed size; best case is the minimum. Average case is an expected value and therefore needs a stated probability distribution over inputs. Amortized analysis instead bounds the average cost across a sequence of operations, often deterministically: an occasional expensive array resize can be paid for by many cheap appends. It is not the same as assuming random inputs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.amortized_distribution: Amortized bounds can be deterministic over every operation sequence.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.worst_max: It bounds the most expensive valid execution.

items.prompt: Arrange the process for deriving time complexity from code.

elements.text: Define the input-size variables and cost model.
Count iterations, recursive calls, and work per operation.
Add sequential costs and multiply repeated nested costs where justified.
Keep the dominant asymptotic term and state the case being analyzed.

feedback.reason: Correct analysis first defines what grows, then counts actual work, composes those counts, and only then simplifies the expression.
feedback.details: Start by naming the input-size variables and what one primitive operation costs. Next count loop iterations, recursive calls, and per-iteration work. Add sequential phases and multiply repeated work only when the repetition is justified. Finally discard constant factors and lower-order terms while stating whether the result is worst case, average case, or another measure. This sequence prevents guessing from a familiar-looking loop header.

items.prompt: Arrange the reasoning for a monotonic two-pointer loop.

elements.text: Identify which pointer movements can occur.
Show each pointer advances at most n positions.
Add the total advances across the entire run.
Conclude O(n) iterations when each iteration advances a pointer.

feedback.reason: A monotonic-pointer proof bounds the total number of advances across all nested iterations, rather than assigning a full scan to each loop level.
feedback.details: List the moves that can happen, then bound each pointer over the whole execution. If a pointer never retreats, it crosses at most n positions. Add those bounds: two such pointers make at most 2n advances. When every iteration advances at least one pointer, the iteration count is O(n). This reasoning would be invalid if a pointer could reset or move backward enough to revisit the same range repeatedly.

items.prompt: Arrange the analysis of a divide-and-conquer algorithm with two half-size calls and O(n) merge work.

elements.text: Observe that recursion has O(log n) levels.
Show the total merge work per level is O(n).
Conclude O(n log n) total time.

feedback.reason: Two half-size calls create twice as many subproblems at each lower level, but their combined input size remains n, so each level performs O(n) merge work.
feedback.details: At the top level there is one merge of n items. At the next level there are two merges of n/2 items, still n work total; the same is true at every level. Halving reaches constant-size subproblems after log₂ n levels. Multiplying O(n) work per level by O(log n) levels gives Θ(n log n). The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n).

items.prompt: Arrange the simplification of O(n² + 3n log n + 7n + 500).

elements.text: Compare n², n log n, n, and 1.
Identify n² as the fastest-growing term.

feedback.reason: Among n², n log n, n, and 1, the n² term grows fastest as n becomes large, so it determines the asymptotic class.
feedback.details: First ignore the constant multipliers 3, 7, and 500; they scale a term but do not alter its growth category. Then compare the remaining functions. n² eventually exceeds n log n, n, and a constant, so O(n² + 3n log n + 7n + 500) simplifies to Θ(n²). The smaller terms can still matter for a concrete small input, but they do not change the long-run classification.

items.prompt: A loop executes once for each of n elements and performs O(1) work per iteration. Select time complexity.
constraints: The loop always completes all n iterations.

feedback.reason: The loop body runs once for every input element, and each run has bounded constant cost, so the total is proportional to n.
feedback.details: Model the total work as c × n, where c is the maximum cost of one body execution. As n doubles, the number of executions doubles; it does not square or stay fixed. Big-O ignores the fixed constant c and reports O(n). This conclusion relies on the stated guarantee that the loop completes all n iterations and that no hidden operation inside the body grows with n.

items.prompt: An outer loop runs n times. For outer index i, the inner loop runs exactly i times. Select time complexity.

feedback.reason: The first outer iteration performs zero inner operations, the next performs one, and the final one performs n − 1, producing a triangular sum.
feedback.details: Add the exact counts: 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2. The division by 2 and subtraction of n are lower-order or constant-factor changes; the leading term is proportional to n². Therefore the time is Θ(n²), even though the inner loop is shorter later in the run.

items.prompt: A positive variable starts at n and is divided by 2 each iteration until it is below 1. Select time complexity.
constraints: Each division and loop body are O(1).

feedback.reason: Dividing by two removes half of the remaining magnitude each time, so the number of steps is the number of powers of two needed to reach n.
feedback.details: After one iteration the value is n/2, after two it is n/4, and after k it is n/2^k. The stopping condition n/2^k < 1 means 2^k > n, so k is about log₂ n. This is why repeated halving is O(log n), whereas repeatedly subtracting one would need about n steps.

items.prompt: For each of n input elements, an algorithm performs one binary search over n sorted values. Select total time complexity.
constraints: Each binary search is O(log n).

feedback.reason: There are n separate outer iterations, and each one performs a complete binary search costing O(log n), so the costs multiply.
feedback.details: Write the total as n × O(log n) = O(n log n). The searches do not share progress in the stated algorithm: each search begins over the sorted collection again. If one logarithmic search were followed by one linear pass, the costs would be added instead. Decide whether work is sequential or repeated before combining bounds.

items.prompt: Two monotonic pointers scan an array of length n. Each iteration advances at least one pointer, and neither pointer moves backward. Select time complexity.
constraints: Each pointer advances at most n times.

feedback.reason: Neither pointer can move backward, so each crosses at most n positions; together they make at most 2n advances.
feedback.details: Charge every loop iteration to at least one pointer advance. Because a pointer never revisits an earlier index, its personal advance count is bounded by n. With two pointers the total charge is at most 2n, hence O(n) iterations. The apparent nesting only changes control flow; it does not create n fresh inner iterations for every outer step.

items.prompt: A divide-and-conquer algorithm creates two subproblems of size n/2 and performs O(n) additional work per call. Select time complexity.
constraints: Assume n is a power of two and the base case is O(1).

feedback.reason: At each recursion depth, the two half-size subproblems have a combined size of n, so their O(n) local work adds to O(n) per level; there are O(log n) levels.
feedback.details: The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). One level has one problem of size n; the next has two problems of size n/2; then four of size n/4. In every case the sizes sum to n, so local work totals O(n). Halving continues for log₂ n levels until the base case. O(n) repeated over O(log n) levels gives Θ(n log n), not O(n) or O(n²).
